claims.text: The proposed test material is an as-processed, bulk, single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Heterogeneous lattice strain promotes unusual dislocation behavior involving multiple kinks and jogs.
Heterogeneous lattice strain promotes the nucleation and motion specifically of edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations are responsible for high strength and strength retention in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
Edge-dislocation activity is responsible for an unusual thermoelastic response in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Increasing temperature causes heterogeneous lattice strains to favor edge-dislocation nucleation and motion over screw-dislocation-dominated plasticity.
Plastic flow in conventional BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys is generally controlled by screw dislocations.
Edge-dislocation processes produce anomalous hardening and modified thermoelastic behavior.
The high-temperature kinetics of edge-dislocation processes directly govern the mechanical response.
Under identical high-temperature deformation, the RHEA will exhibit a higher density of edge dislocations with kinks and jogs than the baseline alloy.
The RHEA will exhibit a distinct temperature-dependent nanoindentation hardness response relative to the baseline.
The RHEA will show altered diffraction peak shifts indicating reduced elastic-strain accommodation relative to the baseline.
The altered dislocation mechanics will increase high-temperature strength retention.
The altered dislocation mechanics may improve ductility.
The baseline alloys have less lattice distortion and therefore predominantly activate screw-dislocation mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism applies above 800 °C under controlled deformation in an inert or otherwise oxidation-limiting atmosphere.
Minor phase transformations or other microstructural effects may also contribute to the observed response.
